OpenAI on Thursday (November 12, 2026) announced local processing and inference for its API in India , allowing eligible businesses and developers to have supported AI requests processed and model computations performed within the country.

The move expands the company’s existing data residency offering in India, which was introduced in May 2025 and allowed eligible customers to store their data in the country. The latest development extends this capability to cover where the AI model processes information and generates responses, addressing a key concern among businesses handling sensitive information.

Initially available for the GPT-6 Luna model, the new offering is aimed at organisations that have not fully deployed artificial intelligence in business operations because of requirements around where their information is processed. This is particularly relevant to customers in financial services with specific data localisation requirements, OpenAI said.

“Some Indian businesses have not fully deployed AI for important work because they need the information involved to be processed within the country,” said Nitin Bawankule, Head of Enterprise - India, OpenAI.

“Local inference gives them more control over where supported workloads run and helps address a practical barrier to adoption. It gives more businesses a way to put OpenAI’s tools to work, and gives Indian developers and startups more scope to build for their own, and enterprise needs.”

Under the new arrangement, both the processing of an API request and the model computation that generates its response will take place in India for supported workloads. Supported customer content will also be stored in the country, the company said.

headline: Prix Pascal: If AI writes your book, are you still a writer?
body: France’s new Prix Pascal for AI-assisted books prompts a writer to reflect on the slow pleasures of making art, loss of individuality, and need to reclaim human imagination
full_body:

There is now a new French literary prize for AI-assisted writing — the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA. The Pascal prize requires entrants to turn in an unpublished manuscript, fiction or non-fiction, in French, of approximately 3,00,000 characters, written with the help of large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Writers must declare which AI model and prompts they have employed. The applications, to be submitted by November 30, consist of “a seed, a manuscript and a technical file, submitted simultaneously”. Ten finalists will be announced on December 4 and the winner will be revealed on December 15.

“This [submitted] work must be useful, or raise awareness, or help to solve in an original way one of the ecological, social and ethical challenges that threaten humanity. AI can now solve previously unsolvable mathematical problems. Here, it is asked to produce a text that will help humanity progress towards wisdom and the preservation of itself and its environment.”

I love the way in which the manifesto strategically reframes tacit support for what goes against the very grain of the creative spirit as an essentially moral and ethical act. But of course! This is the way these things are usually done. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré. The first two are technology entrepreneurs, which too is no surprise.

Notwithstanding their precarity, writers and artists have always been viewed with a combination of envy, fear and hatred. The imagination is a dangerous thing. It is ungovernable. It cannot easily be controlled or colonised. It does not seek permission. And that, to many, is frightening. What better way to colonise the imagination than to introduce AI into the writer’s world? Also, that way everybody — even the ones with little understanding of what a writer does — can acquire the overnight label of one. Where does this leave writers who have spent years honing their craft, writers who have survived by the skin of their teeth? The world needs writers more urgently than ever before, and more of us should let some form of creative practice into our lives.

Two semesters ago, a few students from my Creative Writing course, at Shiv Nadar University, Chennai, confessed to what their worst fears were: that, having come of age in the post-AI era, they would find it a challenge to access and exercise their imagination — which, in their understanding, was foundational to the course. I was struck by their capacity for self-reflection, moved by what they recognised, quite rightly, as an imminent loss. This, too, is the other dark side of what we have got ourselves into: the loss of imagination is foundational not just to the stray creative writing course but to life itself.

The argument that it is best not to be left behind, that AI is here to stay so writers must take the good things it has to offer and navigate the rest, is a specious one. The folks making this argument may be right about the inevitability of AI, but does that make any of it less disturbing or a tad more ethical? I don’t see how one can frame this as anything other than a pure black-and-white story. If you give AI an inch, it is very likely that you will take a mile from yourself.

China denied on Monday (November 9, 2026) there was a spy plot attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, calling the spying allegations unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Mr. Huang has acknowledged to the Nvidia board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing, according to The New York Times.

“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday (November 9, 2026).

The chips company CEO is at the center of a controversy over whether he drove sales of advanced computer chips to China, in spite of U.S. tech restrictions aimed at limiting China’s ability to access these advanced technologies. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft.

Nvidia said on Sunday (November 8) that the company would launch an investigation into the case. Mr. Huang did not name the person in the extramarital affair.

China had previously denied the New York Times report that said Mr. Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that faced claims of smuggling advanced chips into China, and that she was a spy for Beijing.
